q: Which statement best defines a linear axis as an ordering device in composition?
o: A regulating line that must terminate in strong elements at each end, giving it length and direction
A continuous surface or volume that gathers scattered forms together
A center of mass that balances a composition on all sides
A repeated module that establishes visual rhythm
n: Ching: an axis is an imaginary line of length and direction that requires terminating elements at both ends to anchor its visual force.

q: Which best describes how a datum organizes an arrangement of forms?
o: It sets a fixed structural grid dimension for a building
It functions as an uninterrupted line, plane, or volume that collects and unifies dissimilar elements
It marks the endpoints of a directional axis
It balances light and heavy masses around a pivot point
n: Ching: a datum is a continuous line, plane, or volume whose regularity gathers and organizes a scattered set of forms.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways an element can be made to dominate a composition?
o: Making it noticeably larger than everything around it
Concealing it so it cannot be seen
Giving it a shape that contrasts with its surroundings
Positioning it at a strategically important point
n: Ching's three ways an element achieves hierarchical dominance are by size, shape, and strategic placement --- concealment is the opposite of dominance.

q: Simple repetition of elements becomes true architectural rhythm only when what happens?
o: The elements are spaced at least three meters apart
Every repeated element uses a different material
The repetition is confined to a single curved wall
The elements are organized into an ordered or alternating pattern that leads the eye
n: Simple repetition becomes rhythm only when the repeated elements form a structured or alternating sequence that guides the eye.

q: In design morphology, what does the operation of 'transformation' aim to accomplish?
o: Erasing a form's original identity entirely through random changes
Altering a form geometrically step by step while its underlying identity/grid stays recognizable
Disorienting a viewer moving from exterior to interior
Reducing a complex form to a single primary solid
n: Transformation is the incremental alteration of a form while its underlying grid/identity remains recognizable, per Ching's design vocabulary.

q: How can a composition without mirror symmetry still read as visually balanced?
o: A large mass sits close to the center while a smaller mass sits far from it, like a lever
Every element is scaled to exactly the same size
Light elements cluster near the center while heavy ones sit unbalanced at the perimeter
Asymmetrical arrangements cannot be visually balanced
n: Asymmetrical balance works like a lever: a small mass far from the center can balance a large mass near it.

q: When extending a historic library with a contemporary wing, how does the principle of transformation typically guide the design?
o: The architect demolishes the old structure and rebuilds it entirely in glass
The existing bays are reinforced and the old library is converted to another use
The new wing must be built as an exact copy of the original facade
The architect analyzes the original grid and proportions and carries those governing rules into the addition
n: In adaptive reuse, architects study the historic grid, rhythm, and proportion of the old structure and extend those same rules into the new design.

q: Which arrangement is an example of radial symmetry?
o: A row of scattered huts along a riverbank
A long hospital ward flanked by rooms on either side
A tower whose floor plate rotates progressively as it climbs
A round altar surrounded by evenly spaced, identical piers radiating from the center
n: Radial symmetry is a central element with identical parts repeating outward around it, as in a circular altar with radiating piers.

q: How do 'proportion' and 'scale' differ as design concepts?
o: Scale relates a part to the whole composition, while proportion compares it to the human body
Proportion concerns the relationship among a design's own parts and whole, while scale compares it to an outside reference like the human body
Proportion is fixed by building codes; scale is left to the client's preference
The two terms are interchangeable in architectural theory
n: Proportion is the relationship of parts to each other and the whole; scale compares an object's size to an external reference, usually the human body.

q: In the Classical Orders, all dimensions of the column and entablature are derived from which reference measurement?
o: The height of the temple's entrance doorway
A cubit measurement borrowed from Egyptian building practice
A figure the mason selected at random for each project
The diameter of the column shaft at its base
n: In the Classical Orders, the module is the base diameter of the column shaft, from which all other dimensions are derived.

q: Why did Renaissance architects such as Palladio proportion buildings using musical ratios?
o: They believed harmonic musical ratios expressed a divine, cosmic order translatable into architectural dimensions
Deep masonry walls were required to amplify choral music
Musical proportions were a coded way to confuse competing builders
Guild regulations required all facades to use whole-number ratios
n: Renaissance theorists like Palladio believed musical harmonic ratios reflected a divine, cosmic order and translated those ratios directly into building proportions.

q: As a proportioning system, anthropometry is primarily concerned with what?
o: Rates of weathering on historic stone monuments
The dimensions, reach, and clearance requirements of the human body
Humidity buildup inside concrete structures
Wind-load calculations on tall facades
n: Anthropometry is the study of human body dimensions, reach, and clearance requirements used to size architectural elements.

q: The Fibonacci number sequence approximates which classical proportioning system?
o: The Tuscan Order
The Inaka-ma grid
The Golden Section
The Anthropometric Matrix
n: The Fibonacci sequence approximates the Golden Ratio, the basis of the Golden Section proportioning system.

q: What name did Le Corbusier give to his universal scale combining human proportions with the Golden Ratio?
o: The Ken
The Modulor
The Golden Section
The Anthropometric Matrix
n: Le Corbusier's Modulor combined the Golden Ratio with human body proportions into a universal scale.

q: In Vitruvius's triad of architectural qualities, which term corresponds to function and a well-arranged program?
o: Venustas
Firmitas
Commoditas
Utilitas
n: In the Vitruvian triad, Utilitas refers to function/utility, Firmitas to structure, and Venustas to beauty.

q: What is it called when a larger volume completely surrounds and contains a smaller one?
o: Interlocking spaces
Space within a space
Adjacent spaces
Spaces linked by a connector
n: 'Space within a space' occurs when a larger volume fully contains and encloses a smaller one.

q: Which spatial organization has linear arms extending outward from a strong central space, similar to spokes?
o: Grid organization
Clustered organization
Radial organization
Centralized organization
n: Radial organization extends linear arms outward from a dominant central space, like spokes on a wheel.

q: Which organizational system relies on a repeated three-dimensional matrix of structural bays?
o: Centralized organization
Grid organization
Linear organization
Clustered organization
n: Grid organization uses a repeating three-dimensional matrix of bays to regulate form and layout.

q: Edward T. Hall coined which term for the study of culturally shaped distances people keep from one another?
o: Kinesics
Ergonomics
Proxemics
Anthropometrics
n: Edward T. Hall coined 'proxemics' for the study of culturally determined personal spatial distances.

q: Which of Hall's proxemic zones, roughly 1.5 to 4 feet, is typically reserved for close friends and family?
o: Public Distance
Personal Distance
Social Distance
Intimate Distance
n: Hall's Personal Distance zone (about 1.5--4 ft) is reserved for close friends and family.

q: Which traditional Japanese module regulates both the structural column grid and the size of tatami mats?
o: Shaku
Tokonoma
Ken
Tatami
n: The Ken is a Japanese modular unit that governs both the structural column grid and standard tatami mat sizes.

q: What is the term for a beam or slab that extends beyond its support and is held in place by internal tension rather than an end support?
o: Truss
Portal frame
Cantilever
Tie-rod
n: A cantilever is a horizontal member that projects beyond its support, held by internal tension/counterbalance rather than an end support.

q: Which design principle brings every element of a composition into harmony so nothing distracts from the central concept?
o: Emphasis
Unity
Contrast
Variety
n: Unity is achieved when all compositional elements are harmonized around one overarching concept, with nothing distracting from it.

q: A rhythm created by a gradual, step-by-step change in an element's size or shape is known as what?
o: Static rhythm
Alternating rhythm
Progressive rhythm
Monotonous rhythm
n: Progressive rhythm is created by a step-by-step, predictable change in an element's size, shape, or spacing.

q: Which type of scale is deliberately used to make people feel small in order to project institutional or religious power?
o: Human Scale
Monumental Scale
Intimate Scale
Anthropometric Scale
n: Monumental scale intentionally overwhelms the individual to project institutional, state, or religious power.

q: Which design element has no dimension, marks a location in space, and generates all other forms?
o: Line
Volume
Point
Plane
n: A point marks a position in space with no dimension, and is the primitive generator of line, plane, and volume.

q: What term describes a form's apparent stability, based on its shape, orientation, and relationship to the ground?
o: Surface Articulation
Visual Inertia
Volumetric Proportion
Visual Scale
n: Visual inertia describes a form's degree of stability/concentration, based on its shape, orientation, and relation to the ground.

q: Removing volume from a solid while it still reads as the same basic form is which type of transformation?
o: Additive Transformation
Dimensional Transformation
Subtractive Transformation
Parametric Transformation
n: Removing volume from a primary solid while its overall identity remains recognizable is a subtractive transformation.

q: Raising a base plane above the surrounding ground level tends to produce what effect?
o: It hides the space, making it feel introverted
It gives the space a sense of prominence, separation, and claimed territory
It removes any perceived boundary from the surrounding area
It creates a visually unstable, precarious appearance
n: An elevated plane visually and psychologically separates itself, creating a sense of prominence, detachment, and territory.

q: What happens when a base plane is sunk below the level of the surrounding ground?
o: It becomes a monumental marker visible from a distance
It creates a sheltered, introverted zone of space
It increases the structural tension in the plane
It removes all surrounding activity from view
n: A depressed plane forms an introverted, sheltered field of space distinct from --- but continuous with --- the surrounding ground.

q: Which term names the outline or contour that allows a form to be identified?
o: Texture
Position
Shape
Size
n: Shape is the characteristic outline/contour that lets us identify and distinguish a form.

q: Rotating a triangle around its vertical apex axis produces which solid?
o: Sphere
Cone
Cylinder
Pyramid
n: Rotating a triangle about its vertical apex axis sweeps out a cone.

q: Which term, literally 'spirit of place,' refers to a location's distinct character shaped by its geography, history, and form?
o: Zeitgeist
Parti Pris
Genius Loci
Partis
n: 'Genius loci,' Latin for 'spirit of place,' describes the unique character rooted in a site's geography, history, and form.

q: What perceptual effect does a highly polished, reflective floor tend to have on a lobby?
o: It makes the space feel darker and more cramped
It stabilizes the columns by absorbing ambient light
It reflects the ceiling and makes the space feel taller than it is
It sharpens the sense of geometric solidity in the columns
n: A polished reflective floor mirrors the ceiling plane, creating an illusion of greater vertical height.

q: In color theory, how is a 'tone' produced from a pure hue?
o: By mixing in white
By mixing in black
By mixing in grey
By combining two secondary colors
n: In color theory a tone is produced by adding grey (a mix of black and white) to a pure hue.

q: What is the name for a hue that has been darkened by adding black?
o: Tint
Intensity
Shade
Tone
n: A shade is a hue mixed with black, which lowers its value and darkens it.

q: Which color has been clinically shown to lower blood pressure and promote a calm, healing atmosphere?
o: High-value Red
Low-chroma Blue
High-saturation Orange
Low-value Yellow
n: Low-chroma/desaturated blue is documented to calm the nervous system, lowering blood pressure and respiration --- useful in healing environments.

q: In a split-complementary scheme built on yellow, which two hues are used to balance it?
o: Red and Blue
Violet and Blue-Violet
Red-Violet and Blue-Violet
Green and Orange
n: Yellow's complement is violet; a split-complementary scheme pairs yellow with the two hues flanking violet --- red-violet and blue-violet.

q: Which color harmony combines two hues that sit directly across from each other on the color wheel?
o: Analogous Harmony
Triadic Harmony
Complementary Harmony
Monochromatic Harmony
n: Complementary harmony pairs hues directly opposite each other on the color wheel.

q: In commercial kitchen planning, what term describes the efficient arrangement linking the sink, refrigerator, and range?
o: The Circulation Spine
The Work Triangle
The Linear Assembly
The Concentric Ring
n: The Work Triangle links the sink, refrigerator, and range/stove for efficient kitchen circulation.

q: Roughly how much clearance should separate two facing rows of kitchen equipment so staff can pass back-to-back with oven doors open?
o: 900 mm
n: Commercial kitchen guidelines call for roughly 1500 mm between facing equipment rows when staff must pass back-to-back with oven doors open.

q: What is generally the minimum width recommended for a secondary residential corridor so two people can pass comfortably?
o: 900 mm
n: Building/space-planning standards set about 1200 mm as the minimum secondary corridor width for two people to pass comfortably.

q: How does 'personal space' fundamentally differ from 'territoriality'?
o: Territoriality requires legal ownership of the land, while personal space does not
Personal space is a psychological bubble that moves with a person, while territoriality is a fixed area someone claims
Personal space applies only indoors; territoriality only outdoors
Personal space stays fixed while territoriality shifts with the person
n: Personal space is a portable psychological 'bubble' that travels with a person, while territoriality is a fixed area someone claims and defends.

q: Which of Alan Westin's four privacy states describes being present in a public crowd yet unrecognized?
o: Solitude
Reserve
Anonymity
Intimacy
n: Alan Westin's 'anonymity' describes being unidentified and unobserved while present in a public crowd.

q: Why do accessibility standards require strong color contrast between doors, signage, and adjoining walls?
o: To reduce the cost of graphic branding
To absorb sound along evacuation routes
To help people with low vision find paths of travel and exits
To match a minimalist design aesthetic
n: High-contrast signage/door colors under codes like BP 344 help low-vision users identify paths of travel and exits.

q: How can the choice of interior colors affect a room's perceived thermal comfort?
o: Bright pink is known to physically block HVAC drafts
Cooler colors such as blue and green can make a hot-climate room feel less warm
Color has no measurable influence on perceived temperature
Neon finishes are used to trap cool air near the ceiling
n: Cool colors (blues/greens) can lower a room's perceived temperature, helping thermal comfort in hot climates.

q: What color strategy fits a fast-casual restaurant that wants diners to eat and leave quickly?
o: Low-saturation colors, to produce the same restless effect
Vivid, highly saturated colors that stimulate appetite while inducing mild restlessness
Deep blacks and grays to discourage movement
Soft pastels to encourage hunger
n: High-saturation warm colors stimulate appetite while producing mild restlessness, encouraging quick turnover in fast-casual dining.

q: What change marks the shift in royal burial practice from Egypt's Old Kingdom to its New Kingdom?
o: A move from limestone columns to Mesopotamian-style brick ziggurats
The introduction of Roman-style concrete vaulting in temples
Prominent pyramids gave way to concealed, rock-cut tombs meant to discourage looters
Stone construction was abandoned entirely in favor of timber framing
n: Egyptian royal burials shifted from visible Old Kingdom pyramids to hidden, rock-cut New Kingdom tombs (Valley of the Kings) to deter raiders.

q: What technical development allowed Roman architecture to move beyond the Greek structural approach?
o: The development of high-tensile steel alloys
Concrete (opus caementicium) and the true arch, which superseded post-and-lintel construction
The pointed arch and ribbed vault
A shift from marble to bamboo framing
n: Rome's development of opus caementicium (concrete) and the true arch freed architecture from the strictly post-and-lintel Greek trabeated system.

q: Why is the 1851 Crystal Palace, built for London's Great Exhibition, considered a turning point in construction history?
o: It was the first public building carved entirely from marble
It effectively ended urban planning regulation across Europe
It demonstrated that a huge building could be rapidly assembled from prefabricated iron-and-glass parts
It was the first structure to include an electric elevator
n: The Crystal Palace proved that a massive building could be rapidly assembled from prefabricated, modular iron-and-glass components.

q: Which sequence correctly places these architectural movements in chronological order?
o: Renaissance, Gothic, Baroque, Modernism, Art Nouveau
Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Art Nouveau, Modernism
Baroque, Gothic, Renaissance, Modernism, Art Nouveau
Gothic, Baroque, Renaissance, Art Nouveau, Modernism
n: The correct historical order is Gothic → Renaissance → Baroque → Art Nouveau → Modernism.

q: How did Louis Sullivan express a skyscraper's structure in three parts, echoing a classical column?
o: With a decorative, non-structural curtain wall
Through a clear division into base, shaft, and cornice
With an unbroken glass facade that exposed the structural core
Through buttresses that taper as the tower rises
n: Sullivan described the skyscraper's tripartite division --- base, shaft, and cornice/top --- echoing a classical column.

q: Which structural strategy in Le Corbusier's Five Points makes the 'free plan' and 'free façade' possible?
o: Load-bearing perimeter walls of reinforced concrete
A single load-bearing masonry core at the building's center
Pilotis combined with an internal column grid and cantilevered floor slabs
Heavy timber post-and-beam framing
n: Pilotis, an internal reinforced-concrete column grid, and cantilevered slabs free both the plan and facade from load-bearing walls.

q: How does Wright's Fallingwater put 'Organic Architecture' into practice?
o: By mimicking skeletal or leaf-vein patterns in its structure
By using only biodegradable, locally sourced materials
By cantilevering concrete terraces that echo the site's natural rock ledges
By adopting a circular plan that avoids all right angles
n: Fallingwater's cantilevered concrete terraces echo the natural rock ledges of the site, embodying Wright's organic architecture.

q: What device did Gropius use to give the Bauhaus Dessau workshop wing a sense of weightlessness?
o: Thick brick walls pierced with small windows
An unbroken glass curtain wall hung independent of the recessed structural frame behind it
Heavy, asymmetrically placed stone pilasters
A tensile structure of steel cable and fabric
n: Gropius wrapped the Dessau workshop wing in a continuous glass curtain wall set free of the recessed structural grid, expressing weightlessness.

q: Given fire-code requirements, how did Mies still visually express structure on the Seagram Building's exterior?
o: By leaving the structural steel frame exposed without fireproofing
By adding non-structural bronze I-beam mullions over the fireproofed steel frame
With a structural glass-fin wall that used no mullions at all
By casting the entire exterior in raw, unfinished concrete
n: Fire codes required Mies to fireproof the Seagram Building's real steel frame, so he applied non-structural bronze I-beam mullions to express structural rhythm.

q: How did Aalto's Paimio Sanatorium reflect a humanistic, patient-centered design approach?
o: With monumental, symmetrical neoclassical facades
Through custom glare-free lighting fixtures, curved sinks, and calming color choices tailored to patients
By employing harsh, unfinished Brutalist concrete surfaces
With a central panopticon layout for continuous patient surveillance
n: Aalto tailored Paimio Sanatorium's fixtures, sinks, and colors specifically to the psychological and physical needs of bedridden patients.

q: In which book did Robert Venturi argue for embracing ambiguity and contradiction over Modernist purism?
o: Towards a New Architecture
Delirious New York
Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture
The Language of Post-Modern Architecture
n: Venturi's 1966 book 'Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture' argued for embracing ambiguity over modernist purism.

q: What defines the High-Tech style expressed by the Pompidou Center?
o: Concealing the structure and building systems behind stone cladding
Exposing and color-coding the structural frame and mechanical systems on the outside of the building
Ornamental steel filigree in an Art Nouveau manner
Placing most of the program underground
n: The Pompidou Center exposes and color-codes its structural and MEP systems on the exterior, the hallmark of High-Tech design.

q: Which fragmented, titanium-clad building brought worldwide attention to Deconstructivism?
o: The Wexner Center by Eisenman
Parc de la Villette by Tschumi
The Jewish Museum Berlin by Libeskind
The Guggenheim Bilbao by Gehry
n: Gehry's titanium-clad, fragmented Guggenheim Bilbao brought Deconstructivism to mainstream global attention.

q: What material condition gave rise to the term 'Brutalism,' as seen at the Unité d'Habitation?
o: Anti-social, oversized unit layouts
Exposed steel members left unpainted to rust
Rough, unfinished concrete left exposed straight from the formwork ('béton brut')
Demolition of neighborhoods through eminent domain
n: 'Brutalism' derives from 'béton brut' --- raw concrete left exposed as cast, seen at Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation.

q: How did Niemeyer's work in Brasília depart from strict European functionalism?
o: By strictly following right-angled grid layouts
By applying Portuguese Baroque ornamentation
Through sculptural, curving reinforced-concrete forms inspired by Brazil's landscape
By reviving thatched roofs on bamboo structures
n: Niemeyer's Brasília works used sculptural, curving reinforced concrete inspired by Brazil's landscape, diverging from rigid European functionalism.

q: What spatial effect does Zaha Hadid's undulating envelope achieve at the Heydar Aliyev Center?
o: A sharp, clear separation between plaza and facade
A continuous, fluid form where the plaza appears to fold up into the walls and roof
An efficient field of identical flat triangular panels
An imitation of traditional mud-brick fortification walls
n: Hadid's Heydar Aliyev Center dissolves the ground/building boundary, letting the plaza fold upward to become walls and roof.

q: What is a key difference in site strategy between Philip Johnson's Glass House and Mies's Farnsworth House?
o: The Glass House rests on stilts above a floodplain, while Farnsworth sits flat on concrete
The Glass House rests on the ground around a solid brick core, while Farnsworth is raised on steel columns above the floodplain
Farnsworth House is built of opaque timber, while the Glass House is transparent
The Glass House uses stone arches, while Farnsworth uses a steel space frame
n: The Glass House sits on the ground with a solid brick core, while the Farnsworth House is elevated on steel columns above the floodplain.

q: How did the Japanese Metabolist movement, exemplified by Kurokawa, conceive of buildings?
o: As static monuments meant to resist any change over time
As living organisms with a permanent core structure and interchangeable, plug-in capsule units
As mobile structures traveling on mechanical tracks
As purely underground, bunker-like enclosures
n: Metabolism envisioned buildings as organisms with a fixed structural core and replaceable, plug-in capsule/module units.

q: Which of Le Corbusier's Five Points gives Villa Savoye its elevated, open-air living space?
o: Pilotis
Free Façade
Ribbon Window
Roof Garden
n: The Roof Garden is the Five Points element that creates Villa Savoye's open-air living space on the upper level.

q: What forms the central focal element inside Tadao Ando's Church of the Light?
o: A gilded, hand-carved altar
A stained-glass rose window
A cross-shaped opening cut through the concrete wall to let in daylight
Suspended panels of fabric that catch passing light
n: Tadao Ando cuts a cruciform void into the raw concrete altar wall of the Church of the Light to admit natural light.

q: Who curated the 1932 MoMA exhibition that established and named the International Style?
o: Pevsner and Frampton
Henry-Russell Hitchcock and Philip Johnson
Giedion and Banham
Mumford and Jacobs
n: Henry-Russell Hitchcock and Philip Johnson curated MoMA's 1932 exhibition that named and defined the International Style.

q: Which detail at the top of the AT&T Building made it a widely debated Postmodern landmark?
o: An open, broken pediment resembling Chippendale furniture
A golden Gothic-style spire
A functioning, brightly colored exterior elevator cage
Rows of exposed raw-concrete columns
n: The AT&T Building's open, broken pediment resembling Chippendale furniture became the most debated Postmodern gesture of its time.

q: What geometric discovery let Utzon and Ove Arup successfully fabricate the Sydney Opera House shells?
o: That every shell segment could be cut from the surface of a single common sphere
That the shells could be built from canvas stretched over steel frames
That switching to intersecting flat triangular panels would work
That computer algorithms could generate the forms at random
n: Utzon and Ove Arup discovered every Sydney Opera House shell could be cut from the surface of one common sphere, enabling standardized fabrication.

q: What underlies the zigzag geometry of Libeskind's plan for the Jewish Museum Berlin?
o: A direct transcription of a musical composition's sound waveform
A reference to World War I trench layouts
A route optimized purely for solar efficiency
A distorted Star of David connecting historic Berlin addresses, sliced through by a void
n: Libeskind's zigzag plan derives from a distorted Star of David linking Berlin addresses, cut through by a linear void of absence.

q: How did Mies achieve open, flowing space within the Barcelona Pavilion?
o: Using load-bearing marble partitions to enclose rooms
Slender cruciform steel columns carried all the loads, letting the stone and glass planes float free of structural duty
A geodesic dome that eliminated the need for columns
Sloped floor plates that dissolved the sense of separate levels
n: Slender cruciform steel columns carry all structural load in the Barcelona Pavilion, freeing the stone and glass planes to float independently.

q: Who developed the Modulor, an anthropometric scale built on human proportions and the Golden Ratio?
o: Walter Gropius
Mies van der Rohe
Le Corbusier
Frank Lloyd Wright
n: Le Corbusier devised the Modulor, an anthropometric scale based on human proportions and the Golden Ratio.

q: What ultimately led to the demolition of the Nakagin Capsule Tower in 2022?
o: Capsules detaching from the tower during windstorms
A lack of a concrete core, which caused the tower to lean
Deterioration from capsules never being replaced, plus rusted joints, burst pipes, and asbestos
Illegal construction discovered on protected parkland
n: The Nakagin Capsule Tower was demolished after decades of unreplaced capsules led to rusted joints, burst pipes, and asbestos hazards.

q: What imagery did Saarinen's thin-shell vaults evoke at the TWA Flight Center?
o: The rhythm of a factory assembly line
A bird or aircraft in flight, expressing the optimism of the jet age
The spire of a Gothic cathedral
A cavern shaped to muffle noise
n: Saarinen shaped the TWA Flight Center's thin-shell vaults to evoke a bird or airplane in flight, capturing jet-age optimism.

q: Which facade feature of the Vanna Venturi House pokes fun at Modernist ideas of structural honesty?
o: A transparent curtain wall exposing the bedrooms
An oversized, non-structural gable with a split lintel and applied decorative molding
A lone steel column placed in the driveway
An unpainted skin of corrugated steel
n: The Vanna Venturi House's oversized, non-structural gable with a split lintel and applied molding mocks Modernist functionalist honesty.

q: What did Shigeru Ban's paper and cardboard-tube construction make possible?
o: Inexpensive, automated luxury hotels
Fast, low-cost emergency shelters for disaster victims and refugees
The replacement of steel in supertall towers
Biodegradable stations built underwater
n: Shigeru Ban's paper/cardboard-tube structures enabled fast, low-cost disaster-relief shelters for refugees and disaster victims.

q: How does Victor Horta's Hôtel Tassel fuse structure with Art Nouveau ornament?
o: By sculpting iron and steel into organic, biomorphic curves that are both structural and decorative
With plaster reliefs applied over plain brick walls
By hiding all structural elements behind concrete slabs
By eliminating structural metal entirely in favor of timber
n: Victor Horta's Hôtel Tassel fused Art Nouveau ornament directly into structural iron and steel, sculpted into biomorphic curves.

q: How did New York City's 1916 zoning code shape Art Deco towers like the Chrysler Building?
o: By mandating flat, unornamented facades
Through setback requirements tied to a 'sky exposure plane,' producing a tiered 'wedding cake' silhouette
By prohibiting steel construction above the tenth floor
By forcing all new towers to be circular in plan
n: NYC's 1916 zoning law required setbacks along a 'sky exposure plane,' producing the tiered 'wedding cake' Art Deco skyscraper profile.

q: What contradiction exists between the Einstein Tower's appearance and how it was actually built?
o: It has a rigid, machine-like look but was built from stacked timber logs
It was designed to look like poured, fluid concrete but shortages forced it to be built in brick and stucco
It used prefabricated glass panels that later collapsed
It was built by stacking Egyptian-style stone blocks without mortar
n: Material shortages forced Mendelsohn's Einstein Tower to be built in brick and stucco rather than the fluid poured concrete he intended.

q: What three defining criteria did Hitchcock and Johnson set for the International Style?
o: Symmetry, heavy ornament, and regional masonry
Volume emphasized over mass, regularity favored over strict symmetry, and rejection of applied ornament
Biomorphic curves paired with kinetic components
Tripartite massing and classical proportioning modules
n: Hitchcock and Johnson's three criteria were volume over mass, regularity over axial symmetry, and rejection of applied ornament.

q: How does the Ronchamp Chapel break from Le Corbusier's earlier functionalist architecture?
o: It retains a strict, right-angled column-and-slab system
It replaces concrete construction with timber framing
It relies on mass-produced glass panels set into steel grids
It departs from his earlier white-cube rationalism with irregular window openings, heavy sculptural walls, and a curved roof
n: Ronchamp abandons Corbusier's earlier white-cube rationalism for irregular window punctures, thick sculptural walls, and a curved crab-shell roof.

q: What theoretical shift accompanied the Bauhaus's relocation from Weimar to Dessau?
o: A move away from individual craft toward industrial standardization and mass production
Abandoning steel construction in favor of Roman-style stone arches
A new requirement for religious imagery in student work
Relocating underground for tax purposes
n: The Bauhaus's move to Dessau reflected Gropius's turn from individual craft toward industrial standardization and mass production.

q: In what way does the Portland Building's facade break from International Style conventions?
o: It reintroduces a classical, tripartite facade with polychrome graphics, oversized pilasters, and a decorative ribbon
It presents a fully transparent, columnless glass skin
It hangs its mechanical systems on the outside of the building
It uses sloped walls that mimic a pyramid
n: Graves' Portland Building reintroduces a classical tripartite facade with polychrome graphics, oversized pilasters, and a decorative ribbon.

q: How did Venturi, Scott Brown, and Izenour define a 'Decorated Shed'?
o: A structural form twisted into a literal sculptural sign
An underground building left in raw, unfinished concrete
A plain, functional building that communicates meaning through applied signage
A building whose geometry is dynamic and kinetic
n: Venturi, Scott Brown, and Izenour defined a 'Decorated Shed' as a plain functional building carrying applied signs/ornament to communicate meaning.

q: What structural approach underlies Moshe Safdie's Habitat 67?
o: A single dividing wall splitting the complex in two
354 prefabricated concrete modules stacked in an irregular, terraced arrangement
Timber frames wrapped entirely in canvas
Living units sunk into shafts cut from limestone
n: Habitat 67 stacks 354 prefabricated concrete housing modules in an irregular, terraced arrangement.

q: What structural system supports the floors of the HSBC Headquarters building?
o: Thick load-bearing masonry walls
Exterior steel masts and suspension trusses that leave the interior column-free
A regular grid of timber posts
Telescoping piles sunk deep underground
n: The HSBC HQ hangs its floors from exterior steel masts and suspension trusses, freeing the interior of columns.

q: What engineering feature gives Calatrava's addition to the Milwaukee Art Museum its biomorphic, moving form?
o: Masonry shaped to echo pyramid silhouettes
The operable Burke Brise Soleil, a movable sunshade that regulates solar gain
Columns concealed entirely behind glass
Walls built from agricultural waste material
n: Calatrava's Milwaukee Art Museum addition uses the operable Burke Brise Soleil, a movable sunshade 'wing', to control solar gain.

q: What does the move from Modernist linear design toward Parametric fluidity represent in architecture's development?
o: Abandoning safety standards in favor of decoration
Capping podium heights at ten stories
Replacing CAD software entirely with natural-language AI tools
A shift from standardized industrial forms toward flexible, computer-guided, context-responsive design
n: The shift to Parametricism reflects a move from standardized industrial forms toward flexible, computer-guided, context-responsive design.

q: What structural function do the massive 'Earthquake Baroque' buttresses of Paoay Church serve?
o: Increasing usable floor area by moving supports to the exterior
Providing thick walls that absorb moisture for defense
Channeling lateral seismic forces diagonally down into the ground
Physically preventing the ground itself from shaking
n: The Earthquake Baroque buttresses of Paoay Church resist lateral seismic forces, channeling loads diagonally down to the ground.

q: Which Juan Arellano building is regarded as a Philippine Art Deco masterpiece featuring native floral motifs?
o: The Legislative Building
The Manila Metropolitan Theater
The Manila Central Post Office
The National Museum of Fine Arts
n: Juan Arellano's Manila Metropolitan Theater is the landmark Philippine Art Deco building with stylized native floral motifs.

q: What design direction do Juan Nakpil's mid-century civic works, such as the SSS Building, show?
o: Heavily ornamented facades meant to display wealth
Structural expressionism paired with clean, geometric corporate forms
Continued reliance on wood and masonry instead of concrete
A retreat from climate-responsive design features
n: Nakpil's postwar civic works, like the SSS Building, moved toward structural expressionism and clean corporate geometry.

q: Why did colonial-era architects like Antonio Toledo choose the Neoclassical style for public buildings?
o: Because it relied on cheap, lightweight timber
Because it maximized cross-ventilation
To signal Western influence and demonstrate wealth
Its monumental symmetry projected democratic authority and institutional stability
n: Neoclassicism's monumental columns and symmetry were used on colonial civic buildings to project democratic authority and institutional stability.

q: What did Tomas Mapua's push toward a professionalized practice mainly represent?
o: A move away from codes toward purely hand-drawn craft
The institutionalization of formal engineering calculation, material testing, and academic training
Standardizing a single civic and residential design nationwide
Prioritizing residential work over public commissions
n: Mapua's practice reflected the shift toward formal engineering calculation, material testing, and academic training in Philippine architecture.

q: What passive cooling strategy did Pablo Antonio emphasize at Far Eastern University?
o: Deep mechanical shafts for forced cooling
Wide corridors, expansive windows, and building orientation to maximize cross-ventilation
Stack ventilation sweeping cool air across each floor
Shaded arcades and verandas built for durability
n: Pablo Antonio's FEU campus uses wide corridors, expansive windows, and orientation to maximize natural cross-ventilation.

q: How did Carlos Arguelles adapt the International Style curtain wall for Manila's climate at the Philamlife Building?
o: By adding an unconventional interior theater space
By adding thatched, overhanging eaves
By sealing the envelope airtight and situating it underground
By adding exterior aluminum louvers to shade the sun
n: Carlos Arguelles adapted the International Style curtain wall for Manila's climate with exterior aluminum sun-shading louvers.

q: What visual effect does Locsin's cantilevered concrete theater block create above the glass base of the CCP?
o: It channels compression down a shell curve, eliminating the need for columns
It integrates monuments into shaded walkways
It gives the impression of a massive concrete mass floating in air
It demonstrates that thin glass alone can support concrete floors
n: Locsin's cantilevered CCP theater block creates a striking illusion of a massive concrete volume floating above the glass base.

q: How does the stepped, terraced geometry of the San Miguel Corporation Building perform environmentally?
o: By blending modern massing with classical hierarchy for spiritual scale
By enabling a column-free interior using minimal material
By self-shading its own floors and incorporating landscaping to reduce solar heat gain
Through shaded arcades and durable concrete built to withstand storms
n: The Mañosa brothers' terraced San Miguel building self-shades its floors and integrates landscaping to cut solar heat gain.

q: What design approach do Jose Maria Zaragoza's churches, such as Santo Domingo, illustrate?
o: Combining modern structural forms with classical spatial hierarchy to convey a sense of spiritual scale
A column-free layout designed to maximize sightlines to the altar
Floors that self-shade to cut solar heat gain
Shaded arcades built from durable concrete
n: Zaragoza's Santo Domingo Church blends modern structural forms with classical spatial hierarchy to evoke spiritual scale.

q: How did William Parsons adapt reinforced concrete construction to the tropics at the Manila Hotel?
o: By blending modern forms with classical hierarchy
With a column-free plan optimized for altar sightlines
Through self-shading floors combined with landscaping
With shaded arcades, deep verandas, and high ceilings built in durable concrete
n: Parsons adapted Manila Hotel's concrete construction to the tropics with shaded arcades, deep verandas, and high ceilings.

q: What benefit did the thin-shell concrete dome provide at the Church of the Holy Sacrifice, UP Diliman?
o: It blends modern forms with classical hierarchy
It creates a column-free interior, opening clear sightlines to the central altar
It self-shades the floors and integrates landscaping
It relies on shaded arcades and durable concrete construction
n: The Church of the Holy Sacrifice's thin-shell dome eliminates interior columns, opening sightlines toward the central altar.

q: Which macroclimate classification describes the overall climate of the Philippine archipelago?
o: Hot-Arid
Continental Sub-Tropical
Maritime Tropical
Composite Mediterranean
n: The Philippines' overall climate classification is Maritime Tropical.

q: Which wind, blowing from the northeast and bringing cool, dry air from roughly November to February, is this?
o: Habagat
Amihan
Timog
Salatan
n: The Amihan is the cool, dry northeast wind that dominates the Philippines from roughly November to February.

q: Which wind carries moist monsoon air from the southwest between roughly June and October?
o: Habagat
Amihan
Timog
Salatan
n: The Habagat is the moist southwest monsoon wind that dominates from about June to October.

q: Why does high humidity make the air feel hotter than the actual thermometer reading?
o: It speeds up radiant heat transfer
It compresses air molecules and generates friction
It prevents sweat from evaporating, so body heat becomes trapped
It lowers oxygen levels, raising blood pressure
n: High humidity slows sweat evaporation, trapping body heat and making the same temperature feel hotter.

q: What term describes dense cities like Manila running noticeably warmer (2-5°C) than nearby rural areas?
o: Atmospheric Inversion
Microclimate Stratification
Urban Heat Island Effect
Greenhouse Concentricity
n: The Urban Heat Island Effect describes dense cities running measurably warmer than surrounding rural land due to dark, hard surfaces.

q: What problem does a small diurnal temperature range create in tropical climates?
o: Timber cracks rapidly
Wind movement is essentially eliminated
Nights don't cool enough to release the heat concrete/masonry walls absorbed during the day
Solar power generation drops significantly
n: A small diurnal range means nights don't cool enough to flush the solar heat that concrete/masonry walls absorbed during the day.

q: What is the name for the daily pattern where cool ocean air moves inland in the afternoon as land air heats and rises?
o: Land Breeze (Tungkasan)
Sea Breeze (Ambon)
Katabatic Mountain Wind
Cyclonic Monsoon Core
n: A sea breeze is the daily cycle where cooler ocean air moves inland in the afternoon as land air heats and rises.

q: Which building orientation best minimizes direct sun exposure on the long walls, helping keep it cool?
o: East-to-West
North-to-South
A 45-degree diagonal
Perpendicular to the coastline
n: Stretching a building's long axis East-to-West minimizes the exposed wall area facing the intense low-angle morning/afternoon sun.

q: Which facades receive the most intense low-angle sun, making them hard to shade with horizontal overhangs alone?
o: North and South
East and West
Northeast and Southwest
Only true North
n: East and West facades receive intense, low-angle sun that horizontal overhangs (better suited to high-angle sun) can't easily block.

q: Which shading device is most effective at blocking high-angle noon sun on North and South facades?
o: Vertical louvers
Deep horizontal overhangs
Black eggcrate panels
Reflective double-pane glass
n: Deep horizontal overhangs/canopies are most effective at blocking the high-angle noon sun typical on North/South facades.

q: Which shading device works best against low-angle morning and afternoon sun on East and West facades?
o: Deep horizontal overhangs
Reflective double-pane glass
Vertical louvers
Black eggcrate panels
n: Vertical louvers or fins are best suited to block the low, raking morning/afternoon sun on East/West facades.

q: What happens after dark with an unshaded concrete roof slab in a tropical climate?
o: It cools instantly and causes condensation
It deflects downward from thermal contraction
Heat it absorbed during the day radiates back down into the interior
Cross-ventilation speed inside the building drops
n: A massive unshaded concrete roof stores solar heat during the day and re-radiates it downward into the interior at night.

q: Which roof design sheds heavy monsoon rain quickly while venting hot air away from occupants?
o: A flat roof with parapets
A low sawtooth roof facing west
A steep pitch with generous eaves
A single-sloped roof toward the windward inlet
n: A steep roof pitch with generous eaves sheds heavy monsoon rain fast while letting hot air rise and pool near the peak, away from occupants.

q: What is the main function of a breeze block screen wall in tropical construction?
o: To provide shade while blocking airflow
To act as a load-bearing column system
To cut down glare while still letting air pass through
To increase heat gain while venting hot air
n: Breeze blocks perforate a wall to cut direct glare while still letting natural airflow pass through.

q: In solar geometry, what does the term 'azimuth' refer to?
o: The sun's vertical angle above the horizon
The thickness of the ozone layer
The sun's horizontal position measured along the horizon
The vertical distance the sun appears to travel
n: Azimuth is the sun's horizontal angular position measured along the horizon; altitude is its vertical angle.

q: For wall insulation to minimize heat transfer, what should its U-value be?
o: Very high
Low, meaning it resists heat flow strongly
Exactly equal to 1.0
U-value has no bearing on insulation performance
n: Good insulation should have a low U-value, meaning high resistance to heat flow.

q: Why should highly reflective building finishes be used with caution in dense neighborhoods?
o: They tend to absorb too much moisture
They transfer absorbed heat directly into adjacent buildings
They can bounce glare and heat onto neighboring buildings and streets
They tend to attract insects
n: Highly reflective finishes can bounce intense solar glare and heat onto neighboring buildings and streets.

q: Which principle explains why air accelerates when it is forced through a narrow opening?
o: The Stack Effect
The Venturi Effect
The Doppler Shift
Archimedes' Principle
n: The Venturi Effect explains why air speeds up when forced through a narrowed opening.

q: What relative sizing of inlet and outlet openings maximizes the velocity of cross-ventilation?
o: Inlet smaller than or equal to the outlet
Inlet larger than or equal to the outlet
Both openings placed at exactly the same height
Outlet oriented to face the floor
n: Sizing the inlet smaller than the outlet creates a pressure differential (like a nozzle) that speeds up indoor air movement.

q: Which ventilation mechanism depends on warm air rising and escaping through high vents, drawing cool air in through low openings?
o: The Stack Effect
The Venturi Effect
The Doppler Shift
Archimedes' Principle
n: The stack effect relies on warm, buoyant air rising and exiting high vents, drawing cooler air in through low openings.

q: Which window type opens to almost 100% of its area for ventilation while still shedding rain?
o: Casement windows
Fixed glass curtain walls
Jalousie windows
Hopper windows
n: Jalousie windows open to nearly 100% of their area while their angled glass slats still shed rain.

q: Which landscape feature, placed upwind of an air inlet, cools the incoming breeze?
o: A paved lot with no trees
A dense hedge fence
Shrubs planted beneath the windows
A lawn combined with a water feature that cools air through evaporation
n: A water feature or lawn placed upwind of an inlet cools incoming air through evaporative cooling.

q: What passive cooling benefit do wide overhanging verandas provide in tropical resort design?
o: Sealing the building's core off from storms
Shading the perimeter walls from the sun while also sheltering them from rain
Extending the lifespan of building materials
Acting as counterweights during earthquakes
n: Wide overhanging verandas shade a building's perimeter walls from direct sun while sheltering them from rain.

q: Which glazing technology lowers a window's solar heat gain coefficient without relying on external shading?
o: Clear single-pane float glass
Wire-reinforced fire-rated glass
Acoustic glass optimized for high transparency
Low-Emissivity, reflective double-glazed glass
n: Low-Emissivity, reflective double-glazed units reduce a window's solar heat gain coefficient without needing external shading.

q: What material property keeps the traditional Bahay Kubo from storing heat?
o: Massive blocks of coral stone
Lightweight, porous materials with low thermal mass
Poured concrete finished with tuff cladding
Wood panels chosen for their heat-absorbing quality
n: The Bahay Kubo's light, porous natural materials (bamboo, nipa) have low thermal mass, so the structure doesn't store heat.

q: Why is a Bahay Kubo traditionally raised on stilts?
o: To protect the structure and occupants from floodwater and ground pests
To give a security vantage point during tribal conflict
To increase roof rigidity during typhoons
To cut the house off from natural ventilation
n: Elevating the Bahay Kubo on stilts protects occupants and the structure from floodwater and ground pests.

q: How does the Bahay na Bato combine the Bahay Kubo's lightweight logic with heavier construction?
o: By placing a stone upper floor over a bamboo ground floor
By pairing a heavy masonry ground floor with a lighter timber upper story
By using an envelope made entirely of imported sheet metal
By leaving the upper levels without any windows
n: The Bahay na Bato pairs a heavy masonry ground floor with a lighter timber upper residential story.

q: What is the name of the pierced wooden screen placed near the ceiling of a Bahay na Bato to let hot air move between rooms?
o: Ventanilla
Calado
Volada
Zaguan
n: The calado is a pierced wooden screen near the ceiling that lets hot air circulate freely between rooms.

q: What function do the sliding ventanilla panels below the windowsills of a Bahay na Bato serve?
o: Allowing low-level cross-ventilation across the floor
Letting hot air move between upper rooms
Serving as emergency escape openings
Providing purely decorative airflow patterns
n: Ventanilla sliding panels beneath the windowsill admit low-level cross-ventilation across the floor where occupants sit.

q: What is the main advantage of using translucent capiz shells in Bahay na Bato window panes?
o: They are completely soundproof
They diffuse soft interior light while standing up to typhoon winds
They lower the humidity of incoming air
They act as a fire barrier
n: Capiz shell panes diffuse soft interior light while remaining durable enough to withstand typhoon winds.

q: What does it mean when contour lines on a site map are drawn very close together?
o: The ground is flat and open
The terrain is steep, possibly a cliff
The area is at high risk of flooding
There is a buried utility line beneath the surface
n: Closely spaced contour lines indicate a steep slope or cliff.

q: What does knowing a site's soil bearing capacity tell an architect?
o: How much stormwater the soil can hold
The percentage of organic compost in the soil
The required depth of the foundation
How much load the ground can safely carry before it fails
n: Soil bearing capacity tells an architect how much load the ground can safely carry before a foundation sinks.

q: What is the goal of a 'cut and fill' grading strategy on a site?
o: Clearing trees to produce gravel fill
Balancing excavated and needed soil to minimize the cost of hauling material away or bringing it in
Excavating in search of historic artifacts
Compacting soil specifically to prevent erosion
n: Cut-and-fill grading balances excavated and needed soil on site, minimizing the cost of hauling material away or importing it.

q: What is a 'bioswale' in sustainable site design?
o: A mechanical sewage pump
An underground tank for drinking water
A straight drainage trench that simply channels rainwater away
A shallow, planted depression that captures, slows, and filters stormwater runoff
n: A bioswale is a shallow, planted depression designed to capture, slow, and filter stormwater runoff.

q: What design challenge does a high water table present?
o: It makes excavation harder but poses no other risk
Because groundwater sits close to the surface, basements become prone to flooding
It keeps the site's air unusually dry
It forces the use of lightweight timber construction only
n: A high water table means shallow groundwater, making basements especially prone to flooding and requiring waterproofing.

q: In site design, how does a 'vista' differ from a 'panorama'?
o: A vista spans 360 degrees, while a panorama is hidden
A vista is a directed, framed view, while a panorama is broad and open in every direction
A vista is visible only at night, a panorama only in daylight
The two terms mean exactly the same thing
n: A vista is a framed, directed view (often along an axis), while a panorama is a wide, open view in all directions.

q: Why are parking lanes often aligned north-to-south rather than east-to-west?
o: It reduces how long parked cars sit exposed to low-angle sun, keeping them cooler
It makes it easier for drivers to park
It aligns better with the earth's magnetic field
It allows more vehicles to fit in the lot
n: Orienting parking rows North--South limits how long parked cars sit exposed to the low, direct East/West sun, keeping them cooler.

q: Why are native plants generally preferred over exotic species in sustainable landscaping?
o: They typically need much less water, fertilizer, and upkeep
They grow faster than most exotic species
They naturally match a building's roofline height
They are unaffected by solar radiation
n: Native plants are adapted to local conditions and typically need far less water, fertilizer, and maintenance than exotic species.

q: Which site feature is most effective at blocking loud highway noise from reaching a residential building?
o: A thin chain-link fence
An open lawn bordered by a concrete fence
An earth berm planted densely with shrubs and trees
Painting the exterior a bright white
n: An earth berm combined with dense shrubs and trees is an effective passive barrier against highway traffic noise.

q: How is a 'microclimate' defined in site analysis?
o: A localized area whose conditions differ meaningfully from the surrounding regional climate
A regional climate pattern spanning hundreds of kilometers
The overall national weather pattern for a given season
A forecast that updates every five minutes
n: A microclimate is a localized area whose temperature, humidity, wind, or rainfall differs notably from the surrounding regional climate.

q: What is the main purpose of conducting a 'site inventory' at the start of a project?
o: To place orders for final construction materials
To calculate the final rental prices for the development
To catalog all of the site's existing physical features as a baseline
To select design elements and estimate their cost
n: A site inventory catalogs all existing physical features of a site as a baseline before design begins.

q: Why can removing mature trees from a sloped site be hazardous?
o: Because it disturbs the local ecosystem in a general sense
Because tree roots stabilize soil and absorb rainwater, so removing them increases erosion and landslide risk
Because it directly weakens the soil's load-bearing capacity
Because it lowers the water table too quickly
n: Mature tree roots stabilize slope soil and absorb rainwater; removing them raises the risk of erosion and landslides.

q: How would you define an 'earth berm' as a landscape design element?
o: Soil shaped to collect and store rainwater
A decorative stone fountain feature
A trench dug for drainage
A deliberately raised mound of soil
n: An earth berm is a raised, intentionally shaped mound of soil used for screening, shading, or noise control.

q: What is the design advantage of using deciduous trees to shade a south-facing wall?
o: They block essentially all wind throughout the year
They provide food and shelter for wildlife while controlling erosion
They function as windbreaks and privacy screens
They shade the wall in summer and drop their leaves to admit sun in winter
n: Deciduous trees shade a south facade in summer heat and drop their leaves in winter, letting sunlight through when it's wanted.

q: What term describes a broad paved public walkway along a waterfront intended for leisurely strolling?
o: Pleached walkway
Cul-de-sac
Esplanade
Alleyway
n: An esplanade is a broad, paved public walkway along a waterfront meant for leisurely strolling.

q: Which outdoor structure consists of an open timber frame, often planted with vines, that frames a path or seating area?
o: Gazebo
Pergola
Trellis
Vestibule
n: A pergola is an open timber framework of posts and cross-beams, often planted with vines, that frames a path or shaded seating area.

q: Which landscape element is a dense row of shrubs forming a living wall used for boundaries or screening?
o: Fence line
Parterre
Hedge
Bushes
n: A hedge is a dense, continuous planted row that forms a living wall marking boundaries or screening views.

q: What is the basic distinction between 'hardscape' and 'softscape'?
o: Hardscape refers to non-living built elements, while softscape refers to living plant material
Hardscape is living material, while softscape is non-living
Hardscape is designed only by architects, softscape only by engineers
Hardscape refers to water systems, while softscape refers to lighting
n: Hardscape refers to non-living built elements (paving, walls), while softscape refers to living plant materials.

q: What was the core layout concept behind Ebenezer Howard's 1898 Garden City?
o: Endless skyscrapers strung along a greenbelt
A car-centered grid with no parks
A factory complex with housing built on its roof
Self-contained, walkable towns ringed by a protective greenbelt
n: Howard's Garden City model proposed self-contained, walkable towns encircled by a protective greenbelt.

q: What is the primary aim of Transit-Oriented Development (TOD)?
o: Expanding highways for faster car travel
Concentrating dense housing, offices, and retail near transit hubs
Spreading development far away from transit lines
Moving all transit infrastructure underground
n: Transit-Oriented Development clusters dense housing, offices, and retail within easy walking distance of transit hubs.

q: How is 'urban sprawl' typically defined?
o: Vertical city growth achieved through skyscrapers
The conversion of old factories into public libraries
Uncontrolled, low-density expansion of a city outward
Planting forests in the downtown core
n: Urban sprawl describes the uncontrolled, low-density, outward expansion of a city.

q: What kind of neighborhood layout does the New Urbanism movement advocate?
o: Car-dependent cul-de-sacs surrounded by large lawns
Walkable neighborhoods built at a human scale
Mega-blocks connected by wide highways
Relocating residential development to mountain zones
n: New Urbanism promotes walkable, human-scaled neighborhoods in place of car-dependent sprawl.

q: How does the Concentric Zone Model explain the pattern of city growth?
o: As pie-shaped slices following transit routes
As a series of rings expanding outward from a central business district
As sectors that grow along transportation corridors
As growth clustered around several independent hubs
n: The Concentric Zone Model (Burgess) describes a city as a series of rings expanding outward from a central business district.

q: How does the Sector Model, developed by Hoyt, describe urban land use?
o: As concentric rings expanding from the city center
As pie-shaped wedges that grow outward along transportation corridors
As a set of independent focal points
As randomly scattered growth with no discernible pattern
n: The Sector Model (Hoyt) describes land use radiating outward in pie-shaped wedges along transportation corridors.

q: What does the Multiple Nuclei Model claim about how metropolitan areas grow?
o: They expand as rings from a single center
They expand as wedges along transportation corridors
They expand as slices following transit lines
They grow around several independent, specialized activity centers rather than just one
n: The Multiple Nuclei Model holds that cities grow around several independent, specialized focal points rather than one center.

q: What does 'gentrification' refer to in an urban context?
o: The reinforcement of aging bridge infrastructure
Wealthier newcomers moving into a lower-income area, driving up costs and displacing longtime residents
Planting trees along highway corridors
Forced displacement of a community due to war or disaster
n: Gentrification is the influx of wealthier residents into a lower-income neighborhood, raising costs and often displacing the original community.

q: By population, what qualifies a metropolitan area as a 'megacity'?
o: More than 100 thousand residents
More than 1 million residents
More than 10 million residents
More than 100 million residents
n: A megacity is a continuous metropolitan area with a population exceeding 10 million.

q: What role does a 'greenbelt' play in metropolitan planning?
o: Paint used to mark bike lanes
A lawn surrounding a corporate office park
A network of recycled water pipes
A protected ring of open land that contains sprawl and preserves habitat
n: A greenbelt is a protected ring of open land encircling a city to contain sprawl and preserve natural habitat.

q: What was a major criticism leveled at mid-20th-century Urban Renewal slum-clearance programs?
o: That too little money was spent on public monuments
That they demolished historic, low-income neighborhoods without providing enough replacement housing
That they directly caused gentrification
That they caused forced migration due to war
n: Mid-century Urban Renewal was criticized for demolishing historic, low-income neighborhoods without providing adequate replacement housing.

q: What is meant by 'urban blight' or 'urban decay'?
o: Converting older assets into new public amenities
Displacing communities through large-scale demolition
The physical deterioration, abandonment, and economic decline of inner-city buildings and infrastructure
A design trend favoring raw exposed concrete
n: Urban blight/decay refers to the functional deterioration, abandonment, and economic decline of inner-city buildings and infrastructure.

q: How is residential density typically expressed on planning maps?
o: The number of windows per building facade
The number of dwelling units per unit of land area
The ratio of building weight to road length
The number of cars parked along a street
n: Residential density is expressed as the number of dwelling units per unit of land area.

q: Which term names a flexible, master-planned zoning category that allows mixed uses and housing types on a single large parcel?
o: A community where every lot follows identical setback rules
A Planned Unit Development (PUD)
A technical blueprint for a water treatment plant
A park built with a set of identical playgrounds
n: A Planned Unit Development is a flexible master-planned zoning category allowing mixed uses and housing types on one large parcel.

q: 'Land use' and 'zoning' are often confused. What actually separates the two?
o: Land use describes what's actually happening on a site now, while zoning is the legal regulation governing future development
Land use applies only to private property, while zoning is purely an engineering matter
Land use applies to rural areas only, while zoning applies to urban areas only
The two terms mean exactly the same thing
n: Land use describes what is actually on the ground now; zoning is the legal regulation controlling what may be built there.

q: In Kevin Lynch's 'The Image of the City,' what term describes strategic, busy points where paths intersect?
o: Districts
Edges
Nodes
Landmarks
n: Kevin Lynch's 'nodes' are strategic, busy focal points, such as where major paths intersect.

q: How does Kevin Lynch define an 'Edge' in his theory of mental mapping?
o: A highway reserved for pedestrians
A linear boundary that functions as a barrier or break between areas
A neighborhood with a distinct architectural character
A prominent, visible skyscraper
n: Lynch defines an 'edge' as a linear boundary that acts as a barrier or break between districts.

q: In Kevin Lynch's mental-mapping framework, what is a 'District'?
o: A linear barrier separating two areas
A medium-to-large area with a distinct identity that a person can mentally enter
A fence marking a property boundary
A prominent statue placed at an intersection
n: Lynch's 'district' is a medium-to-large area with a distinct, shared identity a person can mentally enter.

q: What does Jane Jacobs mean by 'eyes on the street' as a safety strategy?
o: Windows and storefronts facing the sidewalk let residents naturally keep watch over it
Installing CCTV cameras on every lamppost
Placing a police station on every block
Keeping streets empty and unoccupied at night
n: Jane Jacobs's 'eyes on the street' means active windows and storefronts facing the sidewalk let residents naturally watch over it.

q: What was Daniel Burnham's guiding philosophy behind the City Beautiful movement?
o: Monumental civic centers, wide boulevards, and classical beauty meant to inspire civic pride
Relocating shops into underground arcades
Replacing public parks with parking structures
Eliminating any centralized planning rules
n: Burnham's City Beautiful movement pursued monumental civic centers, wide boulevards, and classical grandeur to inspire civic order and pride.

q: What daily-life goal does Carlos Moreno's '15-Minute City' concept aim to achieve?
o: Spending 15 minutes a day planting trees
Running trains at 15-minute intervals
Placing daily necessities within a 15-minute walk or bike ride
Placing daily necessities within a 15-minute drive
n: Moreno's 15-Minute City aims to put daily necessities within a 15-minute walk or bike ride of home.

q: What does Patrick Geddes's principle of 'survey before plan' call for?
o: A thorough study of a site's geography, history, culture, and people before any plan is drawn
Calculating expected profit before purchasing land
Interviewing officials from neighboring municipalities
Paving roads before finalizing the zoning
n: Geddes's 'survey before plan' calls for thoroughly studying a site's geography, history, culture, and people before laying out any plan.

q: In Ebenezer Howard's 'Three Magnets' diagram, which option represented the ideal destination?
o: The Town, offering high wages but heavy pollution
The Town-Country, combining urban opportunity with access to nature
The Country, scenic but isolated
The Wilderness, with no infrastructure at all
n: Howard's ideal 'Town-Country' magnet combined the economic opportunity of the city with the open space and nature of the countryside.

q: What threat are 'Floating City' concepts such as Oceanix primarily designed to address?
o: Tornado damage
Volcanic ash fallout
Earthquake risk
